svg.title: Caching layers of a WordPress site, from the browser to the database
svg.desc: A request passes up to seven layers. The browser cache and speculative loading serve repeat and next-page navigations. A CDN or edge cache serves static assets and, optionally, whole pages. A full-page cache (a reverse proxy such as Varnish or nginx fastcgi_cache, or a plugin's advanced-cache.php drop-in loaded when WP_CACHE is true) returns stored HTML without running PHP. On a miss, PHP runs with OPcache holding compiled scripts. WordPress keeps a per-request object cache in memory; the object-cache.php drop-in makes it persistent in Redis, Valkey or Memcached. Only what all layers miss reaches MySQL or MariaDB, whose InnoDB buffer pool caches pages; the MySQL query cache no longer exists. Each layer that answers stops the request from going further down, and each is invalidated differently.

g.text: Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified; prefetch or prerender
of the next page (speculation rules, WordPress 6.8+)
Images, CSS, JS, fonts; optionally whole anonymous pages
served from a location close to the visitor
3. Full-page cache (no PHP on a hit)
Varnish, nginx fastcgi_cache, or a plugin's advanced-cache.php
drop-in, loaded only when WP_CACHE is true
Compiled bytecode of core, plugin and theme files in shared
memory; WordPress code runs, but nothing is parsed twice
wp_cache_get() / wp_cache_set() in a PHP array; options,
posts, meta and terms are read once per request
Redis, Valkey or Memcached; shared by all requests and all
web nodes; transients are stored here instead of wp_options
InnoDB buffer pool caches table and index pages in memory
(there is no query cache in MySQL 8.0 or later)

svg.text: Layers 1 to 3 answer before WordPress runs; layers 4 to 6 make the WordPress run cheaper when it must happen.
